title: Moses Sumney - Breaking and Entering
summary: Moses Sumney dropped in to chat with Breaking And Entering and play live in studio
transcript:
Moses Sumney joined Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler at Triple R on 1 February 2018, ahead of his Melbourne Recital Centre show and Laneway Festival appearances. He discusses his debut album Aromanticism, solitude, identity and finding the confidence to share his music. Edited for length and clarity.

Simon: Your debut album is called Aromanticism. In the text accompanying the release, you describe it as 'a concept album about lovelessness as a sonic dreamscape'. Can you tell us about the term aromanticism and how you define the idea?

Moses: Yeah, it's pretty lofty, but aromanticism in a textbook way would be defined simply as the absence of romantic love or attraction. I was interested in exploring that theme kind of in a series of gradients, exploring varying degrees of romance gone bad or romance that's absent, essentially. It's a word that's kind of been floating around on the internet, and I just wanted to give it some shine.

Lauren: But it's not actually a dictionary definition?

Moses: No, it's not really a dictionary-defined word. But as culture goes, I think we're constantly defining and redefining the ways in which we interact, so it's not widely recognised.

Simon: As you say, it's an exploration of ideas that are starting to take shape, and your album becomes part of that conversation. You've said that Aromanticism seeks to interrogate the idea that romance is normative and necessary, but this isn't protest music as much as process music. What does process mean in this context?

Moses: Yeah, that's a great question. In this context, it just means that this album for me is not a definition, because to imply that it is definitive implies that it is set in stone. I think so much about identity and the ways in which we relate to ourselves and others is being in process, being in the process of realisation, the process of exploration. I think a thing that people often miss is that there are people who would define themselves as aromantics who don't ever experience romantic love. As soon as you start opening that conversation, it becomes like, okay, so that's how you are defined. That's your mark, that's your place in the world. I was trying to say, no, I'm not protesting love. I'm saying this is about the process of wondering if love exists for me or for other people at this moment or in the future. It's just kind of about being in process. Does that make sense?

Simon: It does. It implies a questioning, a seeking and a fluidity, which I guess is poetically referenced in some of the metaphors you're using in the lyrics.

Moses: Yeah, I hope so. I can't think of any specific ones, but I think fluidity is definitely the right word.

Simon: I think at one point it might be self-identification as water, perhaps.

Moses: Okay, yes, in the song 'Don't Bother Calling'.

Lauren: I guess that's pretty fluid. Even though you're asking these questions, did you find the process therapeutic?

Moses: Yeah, super therapeutic, because it was real. It was just really honest to kind of go into the depths of myself. I spent a lot of time alone. I spent a lot of time in isolation when I was writing these songs, so yeah, it was therapeutic.

Simon: You spent a month in the mountains near Asheville writing and recording for this record. Apparently you found the first three weeks therapeutic and beneficial, but there was a turning point when it became more of a challenge. Can you identify why it suddenly became more difficult?

Moses: I think that when you give yourself enough time to be alone with yourself, you go through a range of emotions. I'm mostly introverted by nature, so I feel re-energised by being alone. But we so rarely get the chance to be alone for extended periods of time. I found that the joy I got from being entirely alone could not be the only emotion that I experienced over that period of time. At first it was amazing, and then as a few weeks went by, I was like, okay, it'd be cool to talk to another person. Then by the third week it's like, oh my gosh, remember that time when I was seven and someone said this thing to me? You're just thinking about every single thing in your life because you have nothing else to do. It's pretty amazing, but amazing because it's both bad and good.

Lauren: Going deeper into that timeline, as your thoughts and experience of solitude and loneliness were changing, is that reflected in the songwriting? Are songs from certain periods of that month reflective of your state of mind?

Moses: Well, the funny thing is, that first month was May of 2014, so quite a while ago now. That was when I was first conceptualising the album and thinking what it would be about. I don't actually think any of the songs I wrote from that period made it onto the final record. Maybe I wrote like twenty songs during that period, but a lot of that time was spent just thinking and reading and being and existing and entering a headspace. I don't think any of those actual tracks made it, but the idea of aromanticism, what the record's concept would be, emerged from that period.

Lauren: Moses apparently knew from a very young age that he wanted to be a musician, but music-making started for him as a personal, solitary pursuit. Apparently he hid his songbook under a mattress as a child and used to sing to himself under his breath. We jump into the interview by asking why he shied away from sharing his voice and music at that stage in his life.

Moses: Well, just by nature, I was a really shy child. I was very short, which is funny because I'm really tall now. I was really skinny, a middle child, very quiet. My general nature was to not share anything about me. But when I started venturing out a little bit and expressing that I was interested in being a musician and artist—I've known since I was seven years old—I wasn't encouraged by my family nor my friends. I think people's first reaction was, 'Oh, that's really lofty and kind of silly. That doesn't really happen for anyone.' I felt so discouraged by people, and I was already so shy, that I decided I wasn't going to tell anyone I wanted to be an artist and was writing songs. It became my personal vendetta. I was like, 'I'll show them one day.' I ended up not performing anything until I was twenty.

Simon: Apparently you were obsessively drawn to country music until maybe the age of ten. Was it the loneliness and blues found in that genre that appealed to you?

Moses: I don't know, because I was a kid. From my earliest memories of listening to music up until I was ten years old, that was my obsession, period. But I think I was too young to be able to explain why I was drawn to that music. The only radio station I listened to in California was called K-FROG. All of the nineties country I know pretty well. But I don't know. I think I really liked the storytelling of it, and the relation to folk music, which I had not yet discovered, I think I see now in what I do.

Lauren: You grew up listening to Ella Fitzgerald and Nina Simone on YouTube as well. Can you tell us about that time in your life and what you were finding in their music?

Moses: Yeah, it was interesting. Growing up, music was not super prevalent in my household. My parents liked gospel and reggae music, but that was it. A lot of the classics, the canonical artists that most musicians claim to be inspired by, I wasn't familiar with. It wasn't until I was about sixteen years old, that's when we moved back to California from Ghana, and that was one of the first years of YouTube. I started discovering jazz and just fell in love with Ella Fitzgerald's voice, and felt like I could do that on a really basic level, nowhere near her. But I don't know, there's something about the raw expression, and about Ella Fitzgerald in particular, that really moved me. Then I moved on to Nina Simone, and very few other jazz artists started to become a core part of my musical identity, but later in my life because I was already in my late teens.

Simon: There's a deeply contemplative element to your music. Hearing the story of your childhood, and how it wasn't until you were twenty that you felt comfortable sharing, clearly there was a lot of thinking and processing. What allowed you to express yourself musically at twenty?

Moses: Desperation, yeah. Just being like, oh man, I'm getting old. Of course twenty is not old, but considering my peers at the time, everyone I knew who was doing music had been performing since they were twelve or thirteen and learning all these instruments. I didn't know how to play any. When I was twenty I moved to LA to go to UCLA, and right before that I was working at a children's school in an after-school programme. They were all like, 'Oh, Justin Bieber, oh, Miley Cyrus.' They were so in love with these teen artists, and I remember feeling like, dang, I wish I was doing it when I was a teen. So when I moved to LA and finally left my parents' house, that was really symbolic for me. You move to a new city and you can kind of recreate yourself. I was like, I'm going to recreate myself as an artist. I'm going to recreate myself as a person who sings in public and not be held back by disapproval that I'm assuming will meet me. That was a big turning point. I started singing on campus and stuff.

Simon: Talking about identity and reinvention, many songs on Aromanticism feature layers of your voice, almost like a choir. There's a duality between the self and multiples. Can you talk about how you're playing musically with isolation and togetherness?

Moses: I was interested in this record in exploring both isolation and the multiplicities that exist within oneself. Musically, that manifested itself by me stripping away a lot of the instrumentation. A lot of the production process was taking things out to allow for there to be space and allow for the listener to kind of sit with the idea of nothing. That's why a lot of the arrangements are so sparse. But then on the flip side, because I was dealing so much with self-isolation, I wanted to explore kind of every side of myself. The way to manifest that musically was to do a lot of vocal layers. Vocal layering was something I was already into, but I just started to think of it as like, oh, I'm going to sing in a lot of different parts of my voice and stack that in order to say, I don't know, there's multiple people in me. Maybe I have multiple personalities.

Simon: As you were saying before about questioning and not fixing any particular idea or concept, the idea of the void appears lyrically as well. It sounds like Asheville was one of the experiences where you were confronting a little of the void. How does that concept find its way into the philosophy or album?

Moses: Well, I think that thinking about aromanticism is thinking about absence and absences. It doesn't just have to be romantic attraction or orientation, but I think when you feel like you are a bit different than other people in any aspect and you're not connecting, you immediately become aware of what you don't have. I was thinking a lot about that, the idea of a void within oneself existing that has never been filled. How can you miss something that you've never had? Well, if it's all around you, you're aware of what you don't have. I think that's how the idea of a void, the idea of absences, connects to aromanticism. I wrote most of the lyrics up in the mountains outside Asheville, but sometimes in California as well. I was thinking a lot, mainly when I wrote 'Lonely World', because that's the only song that uses the words 'the void', quote-unquote, capital T, capital V. I was thinking a lot about silence, because it's quite fascinating to be in a house alone and you don't hear any other voices. It really affects you, interestingly, psychologically.

Simon: On minimalism, reduction and absence, I'm not sure if this is still the case, but around the release of the album we read that 'Indulge Me' was one of the songs that resonated with you because of its bare bones. It communicates so much with a restrained palette. Can you talk about that as a musical value for yourself as an artist?

Moses: Well, I'm just lazy. I just didn't want to do too many things, basically. No, I'm kidding. 'Indulge Me' is probably still my favourite song on the record, mostly because I'm really into lo-fi folk, really stripped songs. I think it's a good challenge for oneself in songwriting to just have a skeletal structure and allow that to be the final product, because when you do that, all you have is a song. You have to lean on vocals, and you have to lean on lyrics, and you have to lean on chords, which is just the foundation of a song. It was a challenge to myself to be a better songwriter, or at least a better songwriter more suited to my taste. Without adding tons of production and stuff, I wasn't able to be distracted by the computer or distracted by, what's the word? I don't know, auxiliary ideas, and just let it be a song. Does that make sense?

Lauren: For all our talk of solitude today, you've also spent a lot of time on tour with Sufjan Stevens, Karen O and James Blake, for example. You've been invited to write and record with Solange and Beck. How have those musical experiences compared to solo writing and recording? What do you learn in those collaborative spaces that you might not discover on your own?

Moses: Interesting. It's pretty broad, I think, the answer to that question. Anytime you work with someone else, you're exposed to a new process, a new set of ideas, and you're inspired to look outside yourself. I think that's what I enjoy the most about collaborating. It's not really one or two specific things. It's really just the opportunity to have a broadened perspective, even if it's temporary. If you're lucky, you learn something that you can run away with, run away into the mountains with, into your own thing. But I think I like doing stuff alone more.

Lauren: Wishing you all the best for your show tonight at the Melbourne Recital Centre. It's a gorgeous-sounding room as well.

Moses: Thank you.
